prompt: On a certain airline, $10\%$ of flights are delayed, independently. A consultant takes $6$ flights this month. What is the probability that at least one of them is delayed? Round to three decimal places.
hint: "At least one delayed" includes many cases. The opposite event, no delays at all, is a single case.

hints.text: "At least one delayed" includes many cases. The opposite event, no delays at all, is a single case.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with 2 flights: $P(\text{none}) = 0.9^2 = 0.81$, so $P(\text{at least one}) = 0.19$. Same method with 6 flights.
Each flight is on time with probability $0.9$, so $P(\text{none delayed}) = (0.9)^6$. Subtract that from $1$ to get the chance of at least one delay.
$(0.9)^6 \approx 0.5314$ and $1 - 0.5314 = 0.4686$, so the probability is about $0.469$.

explanation: $X$ = number of delayed flights is binomial with $n = 6$, $p = 0.1$.
The complement of "at least one delayed" is "zero delayed": $P(X = 0) = \binom{6}{0}(0.1)^0(0.9)^6 = 0.9^6 \approx 0.5314$.
$P(X \ge 1) = 1 - 0.5314 = 0.4686$, which rounds to $0.469$. Nearly a coin flip, even though each flight is only $10\%$ likely to be delayed.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why not add six 10%s?
steps: $6 \times 0.10 = 0.60$ overcounts, because months with two or three delays get counted multiple times.
The complement avoids all that: the only way to have NO delay is all six on time, probability $0.9^6$.
Everything else — one delay, two, up to six — is the $1 - 0.9^6 \approx 0.469$ we want.
